subject: question about aerial survey data structure

messages.author: bddf776f659aca65
messages.subject: question about aerial survey data structure
parts:
Hi List,

sorry for the lengthy explanation that follows, but I'm working on the
premise of 'more is better'!

We are conducting a series of aerial surveys to examine distribution and
estimate abundance of Hector's dolphin in two large bays on the east
coast of New Zealand's south island. We are using a high-winged plane
and are employing double observer methods (we have based our methods on
Slooten et al 2004, Marine Mammal Science 20(3): 477-490). Auxilliary
information on surface time (to address availability bias) is being
collected separately from an R44 helicopter. We are seeking to analyse
our data using the mark-recapture distance sampling (MRDS) analysis
engine in Distance 5.

The surveys are carried out four times a year, and the project will run
for 3 years. During each survey period, we attempt to complete five
replicate surveys. To achieve this, we randomly choose from eight
pre-determined sets of transects. The survey area is non-stratified. We
do not always achieve the 5 replicate surveys during each period, as
weather conditions do not always allow for this.

I am trying to decide on the best way to structure our data for
importing into Distance. In terms of our Distance analysis, the most
important information for us to obtain is a single, reliable abundance
estimate. It make sense to compare between years at the very least, and
finer-scale comparisions will be considered if there are sufficient data
to do so.

So far, we have completed four survey periods, i.e. 1 complete year, and
we wish to carry out some preliminary analyses. It seems sensible to
structure our data now to give ourselves maximum flexibility in the
future. In other words, I want to try and set up our file structure and
analyses so we can continue to use them as we add more surveys. For
example, we may eventually choose to pool data within years, for a
'between years' comparison of abundance. Alternatively, we may have
sufficient data to look at seasonal patterns in abundance. Or, we may
choose to only use data from the early and late summer surveys for
abundance, as these are likely to provide a sensible 'maximum' (there
may be movement out of the study area at other times of the year).

Having read through some of the material in the Distance pdf text, it
would seem that one option is to have nested layers under "Region": one
for each survey period (see pg 42 of pdf text: "Multiple Child Layers").
However I am not sure this is the best way to proceed.

I also had a quick look at the archives, and another idea
(http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/cgi-bin/webadmin?A2=ind06&L=DISTANCE-SAMPLING&P=R7449&I=-3)
is to define each survey period as a stratum, and for each one use the
total area of the two bays combined. Would the best practical
implementation of this be to post-stratify by adding an additional field
to the Sample data layer (i.e. transect), identifying each transect as
being completed in a different month? (e.g. see page 102 of pdf text,
replace "vessel" with "survey period" or similar, and see para 2 on pg 104).

Does anyone have advice on which of these approaches is likely to best
serve us for now (for a preliminary analysis) and in the future? My
feeling is that the post-stratification option might be the easiest and
best. Or, have I missed the boat completely and is there a better solution?

Cheers, and many thanks in advance,
Sam DuFresne

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: question about aerial survey data structure
parts:
Sam-

Len may be the best person to advise on this with regards to the
DISTANCE interface. I did want to add that mrds is an R package that
can be called directly from R without going through the DISTANCE
interface. If you are familiar with R or willing to learn it then you
can have complete flexibility on how you analyze the data and these
become non-issues. The R package contains code to fit detection
probability models and to estimate abundance from the encounter data and
a fitted detection probability model.. The detection model can use any
set of covariates. Thus, you can fit a global models with whatever
covariates give you the best model and then slice/dice however you see
fit with strata/samples. It will use the fitted detection function for
any subset you want to define. Eventually I want to write a model
definition component for abundance that could accept geographic and
temporal covariates. But that's a way down the line unless some one
else wraps it with the existing code. My only warning on this is that
the R package is not fully documented but t is close.

regards --jeff

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: question about aerial survey data structure
parts:
Hi Sam, List,

Quick answer:

I think Jeff is right, that you have a complex enough study that it is
probably worth your while learning how to do the analysis in R, using
the ddf() and dht() functions that are part of the mrds library. See
the online help topic "Running the MRDS Analysis Engine from Outside
Distance" in Chapter 10.

Longer, rambling answer:

Firstly, I had some possible (minor) issues with your survey design. I
wondered why you had 8 transect sets and randomly chose (a assume 1)
from these each replicate survey. Why not have 5 transect sets and
rotate round them systematically. You don't say how many transect lines
you have per set, but let's assume it's, say 20. One might then think
of 100 systematically placed parallel lines, and on the first replicate
you survey lines 1, 6, 11, ..., etc on the second lines 2, 7, 12, ...,
etc. With your current random design, you may end up with somewhat
non-uniform coverage within the one realization of your design that you
actually perform (of course coverage may be uniform over the area on
average over many realizations, but we only live in the one universe, so
we also want as even as possible coverage within a single realization).
Not a huge deal though. I also wondered how the 2 bays figure into
this design -- does the design go right across both bays and you're
always going to pool for making inferences, or are the transects
separate in the two bays and there is interest in comparing density
between bays.

Secondly, on to your main question. My experience with analyzing
relatively complex designs in Distance is (a) it's rarely possible to
set up a project so that all the analyses you want to do can be done
from that single project, and (b) when it comes to things like variance
estimation via resampling for complex studies, Distance can't do it so I
end up programming it in R or some such package. An example of
bootstrapping Distance analyses in R is given in a tech report by Eric
Rexstad (see http://eprints.st-andrews.ac.uk/archive/00000447/) -- his
code is more complex than what you'll need as he calls the MCDS engine
from within R, while you'll be using the R functinos dht() and ddf().

Anyway, here's what you *can* do using the Distance graphical interface.
You can set up multiple nested layers - e.g., lines within replicates
within seasons within years. You can select out subsets of the data
according to entries in fields - e.g., select out certain years or
seasons. The analysis engines allow only 1 level of stratification per
analysis, which can be limiting. In general, you can use
post-stratification to construct the strata on the fly -- but note that
this option is not yet available for the MRDS engine which you may find
rather limiting. (It's just a matter of writing the relevant data
extraction and manipulation code so if it's a really big deal for
someone I can prioritize it.) For the MRDS engine, you can estimate
density based on a subset of the data that you previously used to fit a
detection function to -- for example you can fit a detection function to
all the data and then in a separate analysis estimate density for just
one year or season or bay (or combination of these) at a time.

Using these options, it should be possible to (a) try a whole bunch of
detection function models at various levels and select one/ones you
prefer; (b) estimate density for any subset of the data you like -
although it may require one run per stratum level (using data selection
to pick out only the data for the stratum of interest - here by stratum
I mean any arbitrary subset of the data). The things that may be tricky
are (a) combining estimates from these "strata" to form estimates at
higher levels, (b) estimating variances at higher levels, and (c)
estimating variances of differences between estimates (e.g., differences
in density between years). The reason is the same in all 3 cases - the
estimates in different "strata" (ie subsets of the data) are likely
non-independent as we often pool data for estimating a detection
function and then estimate density for subsets. There will be no
problem if you estimate the detection function separately for each of
these strata - they are then independent -- but you will likely not have
enough data for this.

There may be analytic ways to get around the non-independence issue, but
a nice omnibus approach that avoids the need for any algebra or hard
thinking is to use a bootstrap. Likely you'll do this bootstrap in
something like R. Search the distance-sampling list archives under
"bootstrap" (there are more than 50 hits so you have to click on "more
hits" in the web browser to see them all) and you'll find that I and
others have posted a few messages that discuss the issue of
bootstrapping for somewhat complex designs (e.g., message 745 - I'm sure
there are others!).

Hope this is helpful. Cheers,

- Len
